Inextricable

/in-ik-STRIK-uh-buhl/ - the stress falls on STRIK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Inextricable means impossible to untangle or separate.

On the oldest survey maps the river's name and the tribe's are inextricable — a single word serving both for six centuries.

Worked Example

The producers hired three engineers to remaster the live album, and all three quit the same fight: the crowd and the band are inextricable. Lift the vocals and ten thousand singing fans rise with them; soften the fans and the singer thins to a whisper. The two sounds share every frequency, taken down on one warm night through one forest of microphones, and no filter ever invented can find the seam.

Inextricable goes past tangled or connected: tangles yield to patience, and connections can be cut. In- + ex- + tricae — 'not able to be worked out of the snare' — promises that no amount of care finds the joint. Use it when separation is not merely hard but no longer meaningful: the parts have stopped being parts.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

inseparable: always found together — mild, and often affectionate

tangled: knotted together, though patience might still part it

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

separable: able to be pulled apart

distinct: clearly two different things

Where it sits · how hopeless it is to part them — linked → interwoven → inextricable

linked vs. inextricable: Linked things are connected but plainly still two things.

interwoven vs. inextricable: Interwoven things thread through each other, yet a patient hand might still part them; inextricable ends that hope — no force or care finds the seam.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: not

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: out of

Root — tric

Root — tric: tangles, snares (Latin tricae)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able to be

Put it together

Put it together: In- (not) + ex- (out of) + tric (tangles, from Latin tricae) + -able (able to be) = not able to be worked out of the tangle. Tricae was the Romans' word for knots, snarls, and petty complications, and it snagged its way into English more than once — anything intricate is folded with tiny turns of the same root. Inextricable is the snare with no way back out.

Use the root in a new word: intricate

Word Choice

formal / analytic

Inextricable is for entanglements past undoing — histories, economies, motives, lives. It warns the untangler off: the seam is not there to find. For knots that merely need patience, tangled is the honest word; inextricable says the parts have stopped being parts.
